analysis.one_liner: Bans sewage treatment plants from bypassing or blending untreated sewage into the Great Lakes.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by a Democrat, never received a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred publicly owned sewage treatment plants from intentionally routing waste around treatment units and discharging it — untreated or blended — into the Great Lakes, except in emergencies. Plants would have to notify regulators of any bypass within 24 hours, post notices in a public online database, and face civil penalties up to $100,000 per day. Penalty money would go into a cleanup fund for Great Lakes wastewater improvements. The strict ban would not have taken effect until 2026, giving plants two decades to upgrade.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live around the Great Lakes and use its water for drinking, swimming, and fishing. Roughly 40 million people draw drinking water from the lakes, and untreated sewage bypasses and blended discharges can close beaches and contaminate source water. The bill would also have created a public online record of every bypass.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes region residents and beachgoers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits sewage treatment plants from intentionally diverting waste around treatment units and discharging it into the Great Lakes, except where unavoidable to prevent loss of life, injury, or severe property damage [S2][S3].
Explicitly counts 'blending' — mixing effluent routed around treatment units with treated effluent before discharge — among the prohibited bypasses [S2][S3].

Requires plants to give regulators advance notice of planned bypasses, notice within 24 hours of discovering unplanned ones, and a follow-up report on cause, volume, and public areas affected, all posted in a searchable public database [S2][S3].

Sets a maximum civil penalty of $100,000 per day for violations and directs that collected penalties fund wastewater improvement, habitat protection, and wetland restoration programs in Great Lakes states [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly owned sewage treatment works and the local governments and ratepayers behind them, which would need backup equipment, retention capacity, or upgraded treatment to comply, and could face penalties up to $100,000 per day.
analysis.who_pays_short: Municipal sewage plants and local ratepayers

drawbacks.text: The main prohibition would not take effect until January 1, 2026 — roughly twenty years after introduction — so lakeside residents would get no new protection in the meantime, only the notice and disclosure rules [S3].

Compliance costs fall on publicly owned treatment works, meaning local taxpayers and water ratepayers in cities with older combined-sewer systems would ultimately bear the expense of added treatment capacity and backup equipment [S3].

The bill authorizes appropriations to the cleanup fund but does not itself fund compliance upgrades for the plants that must meet the new standard, leaving a potential gap between the requirement and the money to meet it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and recreation benefits of keeping untreated sewage out of a drinking-water source for tens of millions of people are substantial, and the notice-and-disclosure provisions are cheap and immediate. The main weakness is the bill's own design: a twenty-year runway before the ban applies, and no dedicated funding for the plant upgrades the ban requires, leaving local ratepayers to cover compliance.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Kirk introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, joined by Representative Daniel Lipinski as cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on June 29, 2006 [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it remained; no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Municipal wastewater operators and the local governments behind them avoided new discharge restrictions, notice requirements, and penalties of up to $100,000 per day. Great Lakes residents received no added protection against sewage bypasses and blending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Municipal sewage plant operators; lakeside residents gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor — and the record shows no opposition; the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Municipal wastewater utilities (publicly owned treatment works)
industries.note: These publicly owned plants are the bill's direct target: they could no longer bypass or blend sewage into the Great Lakes, would face 24-hour disclosure of bypasses, and risk penalties of $100,000 per day. Their compliance costs would fall on local taxpayers and water ratepayers, though the disclosure rules would also let the public see when sewage escapes treatment.

industries.industry: Water and wastewater engineering and construction firms
industries.note: Plants facing the 2026 deadline would need backup equipment, retention capacity, and treatment upgrades, creating demand for the contractors and equipment suppliers that build that infrastructure.
